title: Andre Lamy MPC v. The Queen (2021 TCC) SR&ED Decision
subject: TCC appeal on whether clinical research performed by a physician qualified as SR&ED by his medical professional corporation.
keyPhrase: Andre Lamy MPC v The Queen 2021 TCC
summary: Andre Lamy Medicine Professional Corporation v. The Queen (2020 TCC 61) is a Tax Court of Canada decision confirming that an Ontario medical professional corporation could claim SR&ED tax credits for research its employee-physician performed. The takeaway: signing third-party research agreements in a personal name did not defeat corporate entitlement where the evidence showed the work was performed as an employee.
metaDescription: Review the 2021 TCC ruling for Andre Lamy MPC v. The Queen in the Tax Court of Canada concerning Canadian SR&ED tax credit claims.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural History and Jurisdictional Context

The Tax Court of Canada (TCC) decision in Andre Lamy Medicine Professional Corporation v. The Queen, neutral citation 2020 TCC 61 (Docket: 2017-2714(IT)G), heard at Hamilton, Ontario on December 12, 2019 and rendered on July 20, 2020 by the Honourable Justice Steven K. D'Arcy, is a General Procedure decision addressing the eligibility of professional corporations to claim Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives, and one that turns on its facts, the Court having characterized the central issue as a question of fact. Operating exclusively within the federal jurisdiction of Canada under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act"), the ruling addresses a recurring point of friction between incorporated professionals and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA): whether scientific research conducted by a controlling shareholder-practitioner within institutional, hospital, or multi-centre academic settings is undertaken in the individual's personal capacity or on behalf of their professional corporation as an employee.

The Appellant, Andre Lamy Medicine Professional Corporation, was incorporated under the laws of Ontario on June 23, 2008. Dr. Andre Lamy served as the corporation's sole director, president, secretary-treasurer, sole employee, and controlling mind. For over two decades, Dr. Lamy practised as a cardiac surgeon at the Hamilton General Hospital—operating as an independent contractor rather than a hospital employee—while concurrently conducting clinical cardiac surgery research at his residence and at an office within the Population Health Research Institute (PHRI) at Hamilton General Hospital, while also being employed as a Professor in the Faculty of Health Sciences at McMaster University.
The Taxpayer's SR&ED Claim

For the taxation years ending January 1, 2014 (the 2013 taxation year) and January 1, 2015 (the 2014 taxation year), the Appellant claimed SR&ED tax credits in its tax returns; the judgment refers to these simply as "scientific research and experimental development tax credits" and analyses the claim under subsection 37(1) of the Act, without discussing the specific investment tax credit provisions (such as subsections 127(5) and 127(9)) under which the credits were computed. The decision records that the Minister disallowed claimed SR&ED tax credits of $93,828.00 for the 2013 taxation year and $107,642.00 for the 2014 taxation year, and that the Respondent accepted that these same amounts were spent on qualifying SR&ED and represented salary paid by the Appellant to Dr. Lamy in consideration for his work on the research projects.

During the 2013 and 2014 taxation years, Dr. Lamy testified that he spent approximately 52% to 57% of his time working on four clinical cardiac research projects (collectively, the "Projects"), and the parties agreed that careful SR&ED time-tracking dockets were kept. The technical parameters and institutional frameworks of these four investigations are detailed in the table below:

cells: Coronary Project

Comparative evaluation of two coronary artery bypass grafting surgical methodologies: cardiopulmonary bypass ("on-pump", requiring cardiac arrest) versus "off-pump" bypass performed on a beating heart.

Initiated by Dr. Lamy approximately ten years before the hearing, as an employee of the Appellant; governed by an agreement signed in late January and early February 2010 among Hamilton Health Sciences Corporation (HHSC), Dr. Lamy (as "Investigator"), and McMaster University (through PHRI), whose recitals note grant funding from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research (CIHR); the project was ongoing and not yet completed at the time of the hearing.
Vision Project
Investigation aimed at identifying when a patient has had a heart attack during cardiac surgery; during the 2013 and 2014 taxation years, Dr. Lamy helped design the trials for the project.

International study involving approximately 15,000 patients in eight or nine countries; per the Statement of Agreed Facts (SAF), part of the "Vision study" (which also included the Coronary project); no contract relating to this project was put before the Court.
Compass Project
Large trial testing the medication Rivaroxaban; Dr. Lamy's involvement related only to the small portion of the test population who had undergone cardiac surgery.

Global study of approximately 27,000 patients sponsored and funded by Bayer Healthcare AG (with Bayer Inc. authorized to act on its behalf in Canada) via a clinical trial service agreement with HHSC, under which HHSC managed the project and supervised investigators; Dr. Lamy was one of approximately 600 investigators and served as local Principal Investigator for patients at the Hamilton hospital.
Accelerate Project
Trial relating to diabetes and bypass surgery medication, described by Dr. Lamy as a trial that did not go well; it ended shortly after 2014.
Per the SAF, part of the "Compass study"; no contract relating to this project was put before the Court.

body.text: The Tax Authority's Challenge

Upon reassessment, the Minister of National Revenue (the "Minister") disallowed the claimed SR&ED tax credits in the amounts of $93,828.00 (2013) and $107,642.00 (2014). Crucially, before and at the hearing, the Crown formally conceded both foundational pillars of underlying SR&ED eligibility, through its Reply, the SAF dated December 9, 2019 and filed at the commencement of the hearing, and statements of its counsel. First, regarding scientific and technological eligibility, the Minister admitted in the Reply, and the SAF (para. 7) confirmed, that the Projects constituted "scientific research and experimental development" within the meaning of the Act, as defined in subsection 248(1). Second, regarding expenditure quantum and incurrence, the SAF (para. 9) stated that costs of the Projects were incurred, counsel for the Respondent informed the Court at the commencement of the hearing that the amounts claimed were correct, and the Respondent accepted that $93,828.00 (2013) and $107,642.00 (2014) were spent on qualifying SR&ED; Dr. Lamy's uncontradicted testimony established that these amounts were salary the Appellant paid him for his work on the Projects.

Having conceded both technical eligibility and financial quantum, the Respondent narrowed the dispute to a single issue, which the Court described as whether the Appellant carried out the SR&ED or whether Dr. Lamy conducted the research in his personal capacity—in substance, the corporate nexus requirement in subsection 37(1) of the Act that the SR&ED be directly undertaken by, or on behalf of, the taxpayer. Relying on subparagraphs 10(e) and 10(f) of the Reply to the Notice of Appeal, the Respondent argued that the SR&ED was undertaken by Dr. Lamy in his personal capacity rather than as an employee of the Appellant, and consequently was neither directly undertaken by, nor undertaken on behalf of, the Appellant corporation. At trial, the Respondent argued that the third-party project documentation—specifically the Coronary Agreement and the Compass Letter of Understanding—was inconsistent with a finding that the Appellant performed the SR&ED; those documents named Dr. Lamy personally (as "Investigator" and "Principal Investigator" respectively) and, as agreed in paragraph 10 of the SAF, were signed by him ("Andre Lamy") without noting his capacity as director of the Appellant.
Governing Statutory Framework

The adjudication of the dispute rested primarily on subsection 37(1) of the Act and on the factual evidence before the Court; provincial corporate statutes governing regulated health professions were not analysed in the reasons, but form part of the regulatory background for medical professional corporations. At the federal level, subsection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act permits a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada to deduct, in computing income from that business, expenditures of a current nature made in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada, provided the SR&ED is directly undertaken by, or on behalf of, the taxpayer and is related to a business of the taxpayer. Subsection 248(1) of the Act defines "scientific research and experimental development" as systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing basic research, applied research, and experimental development undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement, while excluding routine testing and quality control under paragraph 248(1)(f). In tandem, the Act's investment tax credit provisions—including subsection 127(5) and the definitions in subsection 127(9) (such as "investment tax credit", "qualified expenditure", "contract payment" and "non-government assistance")—govern the calculation and deduction of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits based on the taxpayer's qualified expenditure pool, which is reduced for government assistance, non-government assistance, and contract payments received or receivable by the taxpayer under provisions such as paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) to (20) of the Act.

At the provincial corporate level, section 3.2 of the Ontario Business Corporations Act (OBCA), R.S.O. 1990, c. B.16, and Ontario Regulation 39/02 (Certificates of Authorization), made under the Regulated Health Professions Act, 1991, govern the corporate capacity of medical professional corporations. These provisions mandate that the articles of incorporation of a professional corporation restrict its business exclusively to the practice of the regulated profession (medicine, overseen by the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Ontario (CPSO)) and "activities related to or ancillary to the practice of the profession". Although the decision did not address these provincial provisions—the Respondent having agreed in paragraph 4 of the SAF that the Appellant's business included researching improvements in cardiac surgical methodology and clinical outcomes—establishing that clinical surgical research constitutes an activity related or ancillary to the corporation's medical practice remains relevant, in other cases, to demonstrating that the research is related to a business legally carried on by the corporation under subsection 37(1) of the Act.
The Court's Final Holding

Justice D'Arcy allowed the appeal for both the 2013 and 2014 taxation years, referring the assessments back to the Minister for reconsideration and reassessment on the basis that the Appellant is entitled to the SR&ED tax credits claimed in its tax return for each of those years. On costs, the Court gave the parties 30 days to reach agreement, failing which written submissions were to be filed within 60 days; only if the parties neither agreed nor filed submissions would costs be awarded to the Appellant pursuant to the tariff.

The Tax Court held that whether the Appellant carried out the SR&ED or Dr. Lamy conducted the research in his personal capacity is a question of fact, which it resolved on the whole of the evidence before it—Dr. Lamy's testimony, the parties' admissions, the SAF, and the documents in the Joint Book of Documents—rather than on the third-party contract signature blocks alone. The Court relied on Dr. Lamy's credible and uncontradicted testimony that he performed all of his research as an employee of the Appellant; on the Employment Agreement, whose recital described the Appellant's business as the practice of medicine and activities related to and ancillary to that practice (which Dr. Lamy testified included his research), and whose section 1.3 required him to devote all of his working time and attention to the affairs of the Appellant and/or its affiliates and no time to any other business; on the Respondent's agreement in paragraph 4 of the SAF that the Appellant's business included researching improvements in cardiac surgical methodology and clinical outcomes; on the fact that the Appellant, and not a third party, paid Dr. Lamy's research salary, with none of the third-party financing paid to the Appellant or Dr. Lamy; and on the Respondent's acceptance that careful SR&ED time-tracking dockets and detailed information packages were kept. On that basis, the Court concluded that the Appellant performed the SR&ED and that Dr. Lamy physically performed the research as an employee of the Appellant.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

While the taxpayer ultimately prevailed before the Tax Court of Canada, a forensic examination of Andre Lamy Medicine Professional Corporation reveals two distinct sets of failures: first, the taxpayer's contractual and administrative deficiencies, which the Respondent relied on in defending the reassessments and which left the dispute to be resolved through General Procedure litigation (the reasons do not describe the CRA's audit-stage reasoning); and second, the Crown's strategic, pleading, and evidentiary failures at trial that doomed the Minister's defence of the assessments.
A. Taxpayer Contractual & Administrative Vulnerabilities That Triggered the Dispute
1. Defective Execution and Personal Naming in Third-Party Research Agreements

The principal documentary point relied upon by the Respondent at trial was a classic corporate governance lapse among incorporated professionals: executing external institutional agreements in the practitioner's personal name rather than the corporate name. In both the Coronary Agreement (executed in late January and early February 2010 among HHSC, McMaster University/PHRI, and Dr. Lamy) and the Compass Letter of Understanding (signed by HHSC and Dr. Lamy regarding the Bayer-sponsored trial), the documents identified Dr. Lamy personally—as the "Investigator" under the Coronary Agreement and as the "Principal Investigator" under the Compass Letter of Understanding. Furthermore, Dr. Lamy signed both instruments simply as "Andre Lamy," and the parties agreed that the research agreements were signed without noting his capacity as director of the Appellant, omitting any corporate execution block, corporate seal, or agency designation (such as "Andre Lamy Medicine Professional Corporation, per: Dr. Andre Lamy, President" or "Dr. Andre Lamy, acting in his capacity as an employee and agent of Andre Lamy MPC"). The Respondent argued that, on their face, these documents were inconsistent with a factual finding that the Appellant performed the SR&ED; the Court rejected that argument, holding that Dr. Lamy's signing in his own name did not change the fact that he performed the research activities as an employee of the Appellant.
2. Ambiguous Per-Subject Payment Schedules and Incomplete Contract Exhibits

A second major documentation vulnerability arose from the financial terms embedded in the third-party clinical trial contracts. The recitals to the Coronary Agreement stated that Dr. Lamy and HHSC wished to assist PHRI by acting as a recruiting centre for the study, and Article 1 provided that, in consideration for the performance of the study, HHSC and/or Dr. Lamy would be paid specified amounts on a "per-subject" (per-patient) basis. Similarly, the Compass Letter of Understanding stated that HHSC, on behalf of Bayer Inc., would pay Dr. Lamy for the services provided in accordance with Appendix B; the Court observed that the Principal Investigator's role appeared to be to pre-screen and recruit qualifying patients, and that Appendix A required the Principal Investigator to carry out the "Study Activity," a term the letter did not explain.

Under Canadian SR&ED rules, if a third party (such as CIHR, HHSC, or Bayer Inc.) reimburses or pays a taxpayer for conducting R&D, those amounts may constitute government assistance, non-government assistance, or a contract payment (terms defined in subsection 127(9)), which reduce the qualified SR&ED expenditure pool under provisions such as paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(18) to (20). Conversely, if the payments had gone to Dr. Lamy personally, the CRA could have pointed to them as evidence of a personal business activity separate from the medical professional corporation (MPC). In reality, the evidence was that neither Dr. Lamy nor the Appellant received any amount under either agreement, and none of the third-party financing (including the CIHR grant and Bayer funding) was paid to either of them. According to Dr. Lamy's testimony, for any payments to be made under either agreement, either he or the Appellant would have had to complete a box at the bottom of page 14 of Tab 4 (page 2 of Exhibit B to the Coronary Agreement) and of Tab 3 (page 2 of Exhibit B to the Compass Letter of Understanding) of the Joint Book of Documents; in both cases, that box was not completed. Furthermore, the study protocol referenced in the recitals to the Coronary Agreement was not provided to the Court, which noted that it was therefore unclear what Dr. Lamy's and HHSC's participation under that agreement involved. Leaving active remuneration clauses in signed clinical trial contracts while relying on an uncompleted Exhibit B box to prove non-receipt of funds created an acute audit vulnerability that required sworn oral testimony at trial to resolve.
3. Overlapping Institutional Roles and Academic Cross-Appointments

Dr. Lamy operated across four intersecting institutional spheres: controlling shareholder and employee of the Appellant MPC; independent contractor cardiac surgeon at Hamilton General Hospital; researcher occupying an office at the Population Health Research Institute (PHRI); and Professor employed by the Faculty of Health Sciences at McMaster University, where his teaching duties included lecturing on research methodology and the inclusion of students in cardiac surgery. Without explicit delineation between McMaster University, HHSC/PHRI, and the MPC, such overlapping roles can invite the argument that clinical trials conducted inside a university teaching hospital using PHRI infrastructure are performed pursuant to the physician's university or hospital appointment rather than as a corporate endeavour of the MPC. In Lamy, however, the Respondent did not advance that argument: the parties agreed (SAF para. 11) that Dr. Lamy's employment agreement with McMaster University did not require him to undertake SR&ED, and the Court treated his teaching as a non-business activity outside the Appellant's business.
B. The Crown's Strategic, Pleading, and Evidentiary Failures at Trial
Despite the taxpayer's paperwork defects in the third-party agreements, the Crown suffered a decisive defeat due to fundamental errors in litigation strategy and evidentiary preparation.
1. Pleading Bare Factual Conclusions Instead of Ministerial Assumptions of Fact

In Canadian tax litigation, the Minister's factual assumptions pleaded in the Reply to the Notice of Appeal enjoy a presumption of validity, placing the initial onus on the taxpayer to demolish them. However, in paragraph 10 of the Reply, the only subparagraphs supporting the Minister's position were 10(e) ("the SR&ED in question was undertaken by Dr. Lamy in his personal capacity") and 10(f) ("the SR&ED in question was not undertaken directly by the Appellant nor on behalf of the Appellant by Dr. Lamy"). Justice D'Arcy characterized these statements as factual conclusions and noted that the Reply contained no assumptions of fact made by the Minister to support them; as the Respondent also presented no witnesses, he based his decision on the relevant evidence before him—Dr. Lamy's testimony, the parties' admissions, the facts in the SAF, and the documents in the Joint Book of Documents.
2. Fatal Concession in Paragraph 4 of the Statement of Agreed Facts

The Crown fatally undermined its own "personal capacity" theory by agreeing to Paragraph 4 of the SAF (relied upon by Justice D'Arcy at paragraph 40 of the judgment), which stipulated: "The Appellant was the medical professional corporation of Dr. Lamy and carried on the business of performing cardiac surgery, providing associated medical care to patients and researching improvements in cardiac surgical methodology and clinical [outcomes]." By formally stipulating that the Appellant corporation carried on a business that included researching improvements in cardiac surgical methodology and clinical outcomes—a business which, as the Court noted, Dr. Lamy, as the Appellant's only employee, necessarily carried out—the Crown effectively conceded the business nexus required by subsection 37(1), leaving its argument that the corporation did not conduct the research difficult to reconcile with its own admissions.
3. Failure to Rebut the Employment Agreement and the OHIP Billing Analogy

The Appellant introduced its corporate Employment Agreement with Dr. Lamy into evidence (Tab 5 of the Joint Book of Documents). One recital stated that the Appellant was engaged in the business of the practice of medicine and "activities related to and ancillary to the practice of medicine," which Dr. Lamy testified included the research he performed on behalf of the Appellant. Section 1.3 required Dr. Lamy, unless specifically set out in the agreement, to devote all of his working time and attention to the affairs of the Appellant and/or its affiliates, and prohibited him from devoting any time to any business other than for and on behalf of the Appellant or its affiliates. Crucially, Section 4.2 provided that any money or securities Dr. Lamy received in respect of his billings to the Government of Ontario (OHIP)—which the relevant provincial legislation required to be made in his own name and under his personal billing number—were received for, or on behalf of, the Appellant.

Justice D'Arcy found Dr. Lamy's testimony supported by this billing arrangement: just as the Respondent did not challenge that monies received from billings made in Dr. Lamy's own name were received for and on behalf of his employer, the Appellant, Dr. Lamy's signing of the Coronary Agreement and Compass Letter of Understanding in his own name—consistent with his testimony that this is how he signs all documents—did not alter the fact that he provided the research services as an employee of the Appellant, in keeping with his exclusive obligation under Section 1.3. The Crown called no witnesses, and the Court received no evidence to contradict Dr. Lamy's credible testimony or the operation of the Employment Agreement.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and evidentiary requirement implicated in Andre Lamy Medicine Professional Corporation v. The Queen against the specific documentation vulnerabilities or litigation failures exhibited by the parties and the governing standard of proof established by the Tax Court of Canada:

headers: Taxpayer Vulnerability or Crown Litigation Failure
Tax Court of Canada Standard of Proof & Judicial Holding

cells: Corporate Nexus ("Directly Undertaken By, or On Behalf Of, the Taxpayer") — Income Tax Act, s. 37(1)(a)(i)

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Dr. Lamy executed the Coronary Agreement and Compass Letter of Understanding in his personal name ("Andre Lamy") without noting his capacity as director of the Appellant (SAF para. 10). Crown Failure: Pled bare conclusions in Reply paras. 10(e)–(f) and called no witnesses to rebut the Employment Agreement.

Question of Fact (Totality of the Evidence): A defect in third-party signature blocks was not fatal where the Employment Agreement (s. 1.3) required the researcher to devote all of his working time and attention to the corporation and no time to any other business, the corporation paid the researcher's salary, the researcher's credible testimony was uncontradicted, and his personal signatures mirrored the unchallenged practice of billing the Government of Ontario in his own name on the corporation's behalf (s. 4.2).
Business Relationship ("Related to a Business of the Taxpayer") — Income Tax Act, s. 37(1)(a); OBCA, s. 3.2

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Provincial professional corporation statutes restrict MPCs to the practice of medicine and "related or ancillary" activities, raising potential regulatory scope questions when research exceeds 50% of time (an issue not raised or decided in Lamy). Crown Failure: Explicitly agreed in SAF para. 4 that the MPC's business included researching improvements in cardiac surgical methodology.

Conceded Business Nexus: The Court did not rule on the scope of "related or ancillary" activities under provincial legislation; relying on SAF para. 4, it found that the research—which Dr. Lamy testified arose directly from complications experienced by his surgical patients and aimed to improve surgical techniques and patient survival—related to advancements in cardiac surgical techniques and treatments and was part of the business carried on by the Appellant.
Scientific or Technological Uncertainty & Advancement — Income Tax Act, s. 248(1) ("SR&ED")

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Clinical drug trials (e.g., Compass) and failed trials (e.g., Accelerate) frequently face CRA challenges alleging routine data collection under s. 248(1)(k) or routine testing under s. 248(1)(f). Crown Failure: Conceded in the Reply and in the SAF (para. 7), prior to trial, that all four Projects met the definition of SR&ED.

Five-Question Jurisprudential Framework: Not addressed in Lamy because eligibility was admitted; in contested cases, Canadian law requires proof that standard surgical or pharmacological knowledge could not resolve the clinical or system uncertainty (e.g., on-pump vs. off-pump bypass efficacy or perioperative myocardial injury detection).
Systematic Investigation & Contemporaneous Tracking — Income Tax Act, s. 248(1) & s. 37(1)

Taxpayer Vulnerability: The study protocol referenced in the Coronary Agreement was not provided to the Court. Crown Failure: Accepted (by admitting paragraph 5 of the Notice of Appeal and agreeing to SAF para. 8) that careful SR&ED time-tracking dockets and detailed information packages were kept, and did not challenge them.

Corporate Due Diligence: The Appellant's careful SR&ED time-tracking dockets and detailed representations and information packages, accepted by the Respondent, supported a factual finding that the Appellant carried out the research (the 52%–57% time allocation itself was established by Dr. Lamy's testimony).
Expenditure Incurrence & Absence of Third-Party Assistance — Income Tax Act, s. 37(1), s. 127(5), s. 127(9)

Taxpayer Vulnerability: Third-party agreements contained payment clauses (per-subject payments to HHSC and/or Dr. Lamy under the Coronary Agreement, a study supported by a CIHR grant; payments by HHSC on behalf of Bayer Inc. under Appendix B of the Compass Letter of Understanding), with the Exhibit B payment boxes left blank rather than formally waived. Crown Failure: Conceded the MPC incurred the $93,828 and $107,642 salary costs and adduced no evidence of any reimbursement.

Unreimbursed Economic Burden: Where credible, uncontradicted oral testimony and uncompleted payment boxes established that none of the external financing (CIHR/Bayer) was paid to the corporation or the researcher (the Court assumed the Coronary financing was paid to HHSC) and that the MPC alone paid the researcher's salary, entitlement to the SR&ED tax credits claimed attached to the MPC.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the judicial principles of Andre Lamy Medicine Professional Corporation v. The Queen into preventative tax and legal practice, the following two Canadian industry case studies demonstrate how taxpayers facing identical structural pitfalls can proactively re-engineer their corporate governance, employment contracts, third-party research agreements, and technical tracking to survive CRA audit scrutiny without litigation.
Case Study 1: Incorporated Orthopaedic Surgeon Conducting Multi-Centre Biomechanical & Clinical Trials (Healthcare / Medical Professional Corporation Sector)
Baseline Scenario & Audit Exposure

Vanguard Orthopaedic Medicine Professional Corporation ("Vanguard MPC") is incorporated under the OBCA and regulated by the CPSO. Its sole shareholder, director, and employee, Dr. Elena Rostova, is an orthopaedic spine surgeon practising as an independent contractor at a Toronto academic health sciences hospital ("Metro Health Network") while holding an adjunct clinical appointment at the University of Toronto.

During the current taxation year, Dr. Rostova devotes 55% of her working hours to two clinical research studies investigating novel titanium-PEEK interbody fusion cage geometries and intraoperative neuromonitoring thresholds to prevent postoperative radiculopathy. Vanguard MPC pays Dr. Rostova a T4 salary of $300,000, claiming $165,000 (55%) as a "specified employee" SR&ED salary expenditure under subsection 37(1). However, the clinical trial agreements with Metro Health Network's research institute and a global medical device sponsor ("MedSpine AG") name "Dr. Elena Rostova, MD" personally as Principal Investigator, bear her personal signature without mentioning Vanguard MPC, and include a standard Appendix B per-patient recruitment fee schedule that Dr. Rostova verbally agreed not to collect. Under CRA audit guidelines, the Reviewer issues a proposal letter to disallow the entire $165,000 claim on the basis that Dr. Rostova performed the research in her personal or university capacity, and alternatively that the Appendix B fee schedule represents a receivable contract payment or non-government assistance under subsection 127(9).
Step 1: Corporate Governance & Regulatory Mandate Alignment

To preempt any argument that extensive surgical research falls outside the corporate capacity of an MPC under section 3.2 of the OBCA, Vanguard MPC must first align its corporate minute book and regulatory filings. Counsel must verify that Vanguard MPC's Articles of Incorporation include the statutory permissive clause authorizing the practice of medicine and activities related to or ancillary to the practice of medicine. In its annual CPSO Certificate of Authorization renewal under O. Reg. 39/02, s. 2(1)6(ii), Vanguard MPC should explicitly disclose clinical and biomechanical research related to improvements in orthopaedic surgical methodology and patient outcomes as an ancillary corporate activity to be undertaken within the coming year. Prior to the commencement of each fiscal year, the sole director of Vanguard MPC must also execute a formal Board of Directors resolution authorizing and directing the corporation to undertake the specific SR&ED projects—identifying the titanium-PEEK fusion study and intraoperative neuromonitoring study by name—while approving the corporate R&D budget and designating Dr. Rostova to execute those investigations as an employee on behalf of Vanguard MPC.
Step 2: Executive Employment Agreement Fortification

Vanguard MPC and Dr. Rostova must execute a fortified Executive Employment and R&D Agency Agreement modelled directly on—and expanding beyond—the specific contractual clauses relied upon by Justice D'Arcy as evidence in Lamy. The recitals of the agreement must expressly state that Vanguard MPC carries on the business of performing orthopaedic surgery, providing associated clinical patient care, and conducting scientific research and experimental development aimed at advancing orthopaedic surgical methodology and clinical outcomes. Expanding upon Section 1.3 of the Lamy employment contract, the exclusivity covenant must stipulate that Dr. Rostova shall devote the entirety of her professional working time, labour, skill, and attention exclusively to the business and research affairs of Vanguard MPC, while strictly prohibiting her from conducting medical practice or clinical research in a personal capacity. Any salaried university teaching duties must be explicitly carved out by specifying the exact maximum hours (for example, four hours per week) attributable to her university pedagogical appointment and excluding those hours from Vanguard MPC's SR&ED time tracking. Furthermore, expanding upon Section 4.2 in Lamy, the contract must incorporate a dedicated Institutional and Regulatory Agency Clause stipulating that wherever any provincial health insurance plan (including OHIP), hospital credentialing board, academic research ethics board, or multi-centre clinical trial sponsor requires professional billings, investigator agreements, or regulatory protocols to be registered or executed in the personal name of the Employee, the Employee executes such instruments and performs all clinical and research services thereunder strictly as an employee, nominee, and bare trustee on behalf of the Corporation.
Step 3: Third-Party Contract Remediation & Financial Assistance Neutralization

To eliminate the contractual defects observed in the Coronary Agreement and Compass Letter of Understanding in Lamy, Vanguard MPC must overhaul its execution of external trial agreements. Whenever negotiating clinical trial agreements with Metro Health Network or MedSpine AG, counsel should designate Vanguard Orthopaedic Medicine Professional Corporation, performing services through its employee Dr. Elena Rostova, MD, as the named contracting party. Where an international device sponsor refuses to modify its global template naming the individual physician as Principal Investigator, Dr. Rostova must append an explicit corporate agency designation beneath her signature, signing as Dr. Elena Rostova, MD, in her capacity as President and Employee on behalf of Vanguard Orthopaedic Medicine Professional Corporation, reinforced by a bilateral Letter of Acknowledgment between Metro Health Network's research institute and Vanguard MPC confirming that Vanguard MPC bears 100% of her remuneration for such research time. Crucially, rather than merely leaving the payment instruction box in Exhibit B blank—which forced Dr. Lamy to rely on oral testimony at trial to prove non-payment—Vanguard MPC must formally strike out the per-subject payment schedule in Appendix B and insert an explicit contractual waiver confirming that no remuneration, grant, reimbursement, or per-subject fee shall be payable or receivable by the Principal Investigator or Vanguard MPC, and that all sponsor study funding is directed solely to the host hospital institution to defray institutional overhead and nursing costs. This contractual waiver eliminates any CRA argument that Vanguard MPC had an amount receivable as assistance or a contract payment (as defined in subsection 127(9)) that would reduce its qualified SR&ED expenditure pool.
Step 4: Technical Documentation & Contemporaneous Experimentation Tracking

To prevent the CRA from challenging technical eligibility under subsection 248(1) and to satisfy the five-question jurisprudential framework applied by the Tax Court of Canada, Vanguard MPC must rigorously segregate routine clinical care from systematic experimental development. Vanguard MPC must retain complete, dated clinical study protocols, Research Ethics Board (REB) submissions, and statistical analysis plans inside its corporate records, thereby avoiding the missing protocol omission noted by Justice D'Arcy regarding the Coronary Project. In parallel, Dr. Rostova must maintain weekly digital corporate time logs signed as an employee and approved by Vanguard MPC, categorizing hours across four mutually exclusive tracking codes: Code 100 for Clinical Surgery and Standard Patient Care (OHIP-billed, non-SR&ED); Code 200 for University Pedagogical Lectures (excluded); Code 300 for Direct SR&ED Experimentation and Analysis (formulating hypotheses, analyzing biomechanical cage subsidence failure modes, and evaluating perioperative neuromonitoring data anomalies); and Code 400 for Routine Clinical Trial Administration (standard patient consent intake, treated as non-SR&ED routine activity—for example, routine data collection excluded under paragraph 248(1)(k)). Finally, because dividends paid to a shareholder do not constitute salary or wages incurred under subsection 37(1), Vanguard MPC must remunerate Dr. Rostova via regular payroll with statutory source deductions remitted to the CRA and reported on a T4 slip, while adhering to the "specified employee" rules under subsections 37(9) and 37(9.1), which exclude bonuses and remuneration based on profits and cap claimable SR&ED salary or wages at five times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE).
Case Study 2: Principal Engineer-Shareholder Conducting Consortium R&D Across Corporate and University Lab Environments (Advanced Engineering & CleanTech Sector)
Baseline Scenario & Audit Exposure

Borealis Computational Fluid Dynamics Inc. ("Borealis CFD") is a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) based in Calgary, Alberta, specializing in multiphase pipeline flow assurance and supercritical CO2 turbomachinery design. Its founder, sole director, and controlling shareholder, Dr. Marcus Vance, P.Eng., is a PhD mechanical engineer who also holds an Adjunct Research Professorship at a major Canadian university ("Western Tech University").

During the taxation year, Borealis CFD claims $140,000 of Dr. Vance's $200,000 T4 salary (70% time allocation) for an experimental development project aimed at resolving acoustic cavitation and phase-change instabilities in high-pressure supercritical CO2 impellers. To validate the computational models against physical test-rig telemetry, Dr. Vance utilizes a high-pressure flow loop located inside Western Tech University's Turbomachinery Lab under a Multi-Party Industrial Consortium Research Agreement funded in part by a Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) Alliance grant and two midstream pipeline operators. Because Western Tech University's Research Services Office utilizes standard academic grant templates, Dr. Vance signed the Consortium Agreement in his personal name ("Dr. Marcus Vance, Principal Investigator") without referencing Borealis CFD. Upon audit, the CRA disallows Borealis CFD's entire SR&ED claim, asserting that the physical experimentation at the university lab was performed by Dr. Vance personally as an academic researcher rather than by Borealis CFD under subsection 37(1), that Borealis CFD cannot prove it holds the right to exploit the resulting intellectual property, and that the NSERC and industry consortium funds paid to the university taint the project as funded research.
Step 1: Corporate Governance & Commercial Exploitation Nexus

Unlike a regulated medical corporation relying on provincial "ancillary activities" provisions, an engineering CCPC must demonstrate that the SR&ED is directly related to a commercial business carried on by the corporation and that the corporation holds the legal right to commercially exploit the resulting technological advancement. Prior to initiating the supercritical CO2 impeller investigation, Borealis CFD's Board of Directors must adopt a formal Corporate R&D Project Charter defining exactly how the resulting computational fluid dynamics (CFD) algorithms and impeller blade geometries will be integrated into Borealis CFD's commercial software licensing and engineering consulting offerings in Canada. Concurrently, Dr. Vance and Borealis CFD must execute a comprehensive Intellectual Property Assignment and Exploitation Agreement confirming that all algorithms, simulation code, mathematical models, and experimental know-how developed by Dr. Vance during his employment vest ab initio in Borealis CFD, and that Borealis CFD retains an irrevocable, royalty-free commercial licence to exploit any foreground intellectual property generated during the consortium validation trials.
Step 2: Employment Agreement & Dual-Capacity Segregation

To insulate Borealis CFD against the CRA's allegation that Dr. Vance acted in his personal academic capacity, Borealis CFD must execute a binding Executive Employment and Technical Services Agreement incorporating the core structural safeguards established in Lamy. Mirroring Section 1.3 in Lamy, the agreement must require Dr. Vance to devote 100% of his commercial and engineering working time exclusively to Borealis CFD, while explicitly defining his Adjunct Professorship at Western Tech University as an unpaid, non-commercial honorary appointment (or capping any university graduate student supervision at a fixed de minimis threshold performed strictly outside corporate working hours). Extending the logic of Section 4.2 in Lamy (which addressed monies received from billings made in Dr. Lamy's own name), the agreement must also include an express Nominee Execution and Facility Access Mandate establishing that whenever Dr. Vance executes university laboratory access agreements, academic consortium documents, or safety protocols in his personal name, he does so strictly under the direction and control of Borealis CFD as its employee and agent, for the sole purpose of testing and validating Borealis CFD's proprietary engineering hypotheses.
Step 3: Consortium Contract Restructuring & Grant Insulation

To prevent third-party academic grant templates from severing corporate nexus or triggering assistance reductions under subsections 127(18) to (20), Borealis CFD must proactively restructure its external consortium documentation. The Multi-Party Industrial Consortium Agreement must be amended via a formal joinder addendum to name Borealis Computational Fluid Dynamics Inc. explicitly as an "Industrial Collaborator" party, designating Dr. Marcus Vance as Corporate Principal Investigator acting in his capacity as President and Employee of Borealis Computational Fluid Dynamics Inc. Furthermore, improving upon the uncompleted Exhibit B payment box in Lamy, the Consortium Agreement must incorporate an explicit Financial Demarcation Schedule confirming that 100% of the NSERC grant and pipeline operator cash contributions are paid to and retained exclusively by Western Tech University to fund graduate student stipends and physical test-rig consumables, and that zero dollars ($0.00) are paid, reimbursed, or credited to Borealis CFD or Dr. Vance. This contractual ring-fencing proves conclusively that Borealis CFD bore the unassisted economic cost of Dr. Vance's $140,000 SR&ED salary.
Step 4: Systematic Investigation & Contemporaneous Technical Tracking

To substantiate both the subsection 248(1) technological advancement and the corporate performance of the SR&ED, Borealis CFD must maintain corporate-branded technical records throughout the project lifecycle. All CFD solver code commits, mesh sensitivity analyses, and test-rig telemetry evaluations must be logged inside Borealis CFD's corporate Git repository and corporate cloud environment under corporate credentials rather than university accounts. Each iterative test cycle must be contemporaneously recorded in a corporate SR&ED Technical Log that documents the specific technological uncertainty (such as the inability of standard Navier-Stokes two-phase barotropic models to predict acoustic shockwave formation near the thermodynamic critical point of CO2 at approximately 31.1 °C (304.1 K) and 7.38 MPa), the formulated engineering hypothesis, the boundary conditions executed in the CFD code and physical flow loop, the observed analytical deviation, and the resulting incremental technological advancement in multiphase flow modelling.
Comparative Remediation Matrix Across Both Case Studies

The table below synthesizes the exact operational transformations required across both case studies to convert the audit vulnerabilities exposed in Andre Lamy Medicine Professional Corporation into an unassailable SR&ED compliance posture:

Remediated Best-Practice Posture (Satisfying TCC & CRA Standards)

Articles of Incorporation and College filings explicitly authorize ancillary research; annual Board Resolutions formally approve specific SR&ED projects and budgets.
Employment Agreement Terms (s. 37(1)(a)(i) Corporate Nexus)
Informal or unwritten employment arrangement between the controlling shareholder and their corporation; ambiguous split between personal/academic roles and corporate duties.

Written Employment Agreement binding the researcher to devote all of his or her working time exclusively to the corporation (modelled on s. 1.3 in Lamy) and deeming all personal signatures and billings to be executed as bare trustee and agent for the corporation (an expansion of s. 4.2 in Lamy, which addressed only monies received from billings made in the practitioner's own name).
Third-Party Contract Execution (Contractual Capacity)
Researcher signs hospital, university, or pharmaceutical clinical trial agreements in their personal name ("Andre Lamy") with no mention of the corporation.

Corporation is named directly as a contracting party, or the researcher signs with an explicit corporate agency block ("acting as President and Employee on behalf of [Corporation]") supported by an institutional acknowledgment letter.
Third-Party Grant & Fee Schedules (s. 127(9) Assistance Rules)

Time & Technical Documentation (s. 248(1) & Quantum Proof)

Contemporaneous weekly corporate time-tracking dockets segregating eligible SR&ED experimentation from routine clinical or pedagogical work, backed by complete protocols and corporate-hosted experimental logs.

body.text: 5. Conclusions and Strategic Recommendations for Canadian Tax Practitioners

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Andre Lamy Medicine Professional Corporation v. The Queen (2020 TCC 61) illustrates a practical point for Canadian R&D tax practice: on the question of fact of who carried out the SR&ED, the Court looked to the substance of the evidence as a whole rather than to the administrative form of third-party signature blocks. Justice D'Arcy's holding shows that where a corporation has a written employment agreement requiring its professional shareholder-employee to devote all of his working time to the corporation's business, bears the economic burden of the researcher's salary without external reimbursement, and maintains careful SR&ED time-tracking dockets—and where the researcher's credible testimony is uncontradicted—the mere fact that third-party institutional or clinical trial agreements bear the practitioner's personal signature did not defeat the corporation's entitlement to the SR&ED tax credits claimed, the SR&ED having been directly undertaken by the corporation for the purposes of subsection 37(1).

Nevertheless, Canadian tax counsel and technical advisors must recognize that the Appellant in Lamy prevailed in large part because the Crown had already conceded technical eligibility under subsection 248(1), stipulated in Paragraph 4 of the SAF that the corporation's business included researching improvements in cardiac surgical methodology, and called no witnesses and adduced no evidence to contradict Dr. Lamy's testimony or the Employment Agreement. In contemporary CRA audits of MPCs, Dental Professional Corporations (DPCs), and owner-managed engineering consultancies, the CRA actively challenges both the corporate nexus and the underlying five-question scientific eligibility framework. By proactively implementing written exclusive employment agreements containing explicit agency trust clauses, executing tripartite institutional acknowledgments, formally waiving third-party per-subject fee schedules, and maintaining rigorous contemporaneous time and hypothesis logs, Canadian corporations can secure their SR&ED tax incentives at the audit stage without incurring the expense and uncertainty of Tax Court litigation.

outcome: Appeal allowed; court held the doctor's research activities were directly undertaken on behalf of the corporation and eligible.
